stem:
A small crystal is made to vibrate with simple harmonic motion. The variation with time *t* of the displacement *x* of one surface of the crystal from its equilibrium position is shown in Fig. 4.1.

[[fig:f1]]

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the angular frequency of the vibration of the surface is 4.2 × 10⁷ rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Determine the maximum acceleration *a*₀ of the vibration of the surface.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The crystal may be modelled as a single mass of 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ kg that vibrates as shown in Fig. 4.1.

Calculate the total energy *E* of the vibrations.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.lead: The crystal generates ultrasound waves that are used to obtain diagnostic information about internal structures.
parts.text:
The crystal is made from piezoelectric material.

Explain how the crystal is made to vibrate.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text:
A parallel beam of ultrasound waves is incident on a muscle-bone boundary. Data for muscle and bone are given in Table 4.1.

[[fig:f2]]

Calculate the percentage of the intensity of the ultrasound beam that is transmitted at this boundary.

figures.caption: Fig. 4.1
figures.alt: A displacement–time graph showing a sinusoidal oscillation, with displacement x in 10⁻⁶ m and time t in 10⁻⁶ s.

figures.caption: Table 4.1
figures.alt: A table giving density and speed of sound for muscle (1100 kg m⁻³, 1600 m s⁻¹) and bone (1900 kg m⁻³, 4100 m s⁻¹).
